cases.evidence: Piece '정도' alone rendered as nonsensical 'degree'; contradiction stayed high (0.70→0.59) through the next two pieces too.
cases.cause: bare quantifier/degree word cut off before the noun or clause it modifies had arrived
cases.proposed_rule: Do not place a boundary right after a bare degree/quantifier word (e.g. 정도, 만큼, 정도는) that still needs a following head noun or verb to be meaningful; keep it attached to that head.

example_pair.output: 했을 때 정도 <SEG:1> 군대를 다녀오고 나서 <SEG:2> 유언 그거...

cases.evidence: contradiction_after_each_piece[0]=0.917 even though the human judgement called it safe; the vocative's grammatical role (address vs subject) was not yet settled.
cases.cause: bare proper noun with ambiguous syntactic role (vocative vs subject) not disambiguated until the verb of the next clause
cases.proposed_rule: Do not end a piece right after a bare name/proper noun when nothing yet shows whether it is a vocative or the clause subject; wait for the verb/particle that fixes its role.

cases.evidence: Oracle renders slang '고인물' literally as 'stagnant water', which lowers adequacy for reasons unrelated to any boundary choice.
cases.cause: idiomatic/slang term mistranslated literally in the reference translation itself
cases.proposed_rule: When low adequacy traces to a literal rendering of an idiom/slang term that is wrong in the oracle itself, flag reference_suspect instead of altering segmentation.

cases.evidence: Judgement explicitly flags 전과 as mistranslated in the oracle (criminal record vs change-of-major); this drives the spurious 0.7255 contradiction at boundary 0 even though that piece is fine.
cases.cause: homograph mistranslated in the reference, producing a false contradiction signal unrelated to segmentation
cases.proposed_rule: When a high contradiction score coincides with a homograph/ambiguous lexical item mistranslated in the oracle, mark reference_suspect and exclude that boundary from placement/priority scoring.

cases.evidence: Adequacy drops from 0.7204 (T3) to 0.5892 (T6): the boundary after '그러면은' that survives at the tight budget strands '올리는' from its temporal frame, giving the odd 'Raising.' rendering; the safer boundary at the following full stop only survives at T3.
cases.cause: clause-final adverbial connective (-면은) ranked above the sentence-final boundary that would keep the predicate intact
cases.proposed_rule: Rank a boundary that separates a clause-final adverbial/conditional connective (e.g. -면은, -다면) from its predicate lower than the boundary at the following sentence-final punctuation, since splitting there strands the verb without its temporal/modal cue.

example_pair.input: 내일은 그러면은 올리는. 근데 그거 올 차 사이트에 올리고서
example_pair.output: 내일은 그러면은 올리는. <SEG:1> 근데 <SEG:2> 그거 <SEG:3> 올 차 사이트에 <SEG:4> 올리고서

summary: Most failures are placement errors where a boundary lands before the modifying head or disambiguating verb arrives, producing literal/nonsensical fragments even though the later contradiction score looks fine to a judge; two cases are actually bad oracles (slang/homograph mistranslated) rather than segmentation faults; one case shows a genuine priority problem where a boundary that severs a connective from its predicate is ranked above a safer sentence-final boundary.
